title: Manchester United making ‘lot of progress’ with new Old Trafford, says stadium CEO
content:
Manchester United have said that they are making “a lot of progress” on building a new, 100,000-capacity stadium, in the first official update since plans were unveiled just over a year ago.

Collette Roche, United’s chief executive of new stadium development, told the club’s official podcast that they hope to be able to share developments on land assembly within the “next few months”.

United’s ambitious designs for a canopy roof rely upon purchasing land to the west of Old Trafford, which is currently the site of a rail freight terminal. The terminal is operated by Freightliner Ltd. United valued the land within the region of £50million ($67m), far below Freightliner’s demands of £400m in negotiations last year.

Last September, The Athletic revealed that the impasse in talks had led to United drawing up plans to scrap the canopy, but Roche is optimistic that agreements can be found with local landowners.

“We’ve made a lot of progress in the last twelve months. A lot of it has been behind the scenes, so people might not have seen that,” she told the club’s official podcast.

“We want to make sure we get the best possible position for this stadium, one which has got plenty of land around it to put the right facilities in place, one that’s connected and offers a great match day experience.

“I’ve been spending a lot of time talking to all the local landowners to understand where that needs to be, and we’re progressing that really, really well, and I’m hoping to be able to share some positive news on that front in the next few months.”

Aside from land assembly, financing is another outstanding question regarding United’s plans for a new build, which carried an estimated £2bn cost.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe, United’s co-owner, said the project was “eminently financeable” last year, and “definitely deliverable” provided that it was part of a wider regeneration scheme funded by the UK government.

United have consistently said that no public money will be sought to finance the construction of the stadium itself, a message reiterated at the club’s most recent fans’ forum earlier this month.

The project is all but certain to involve the club borrowing money, however. United’s total financial debt stood at £777m in their latest set of financial accounts.

“I’m delighted to say we’ve had a lot of interest,” Roche said regarding potential financing for the project. “There are a lot of people and organisations that want to invest, not just in the stadium, but also in the wider stadium district, and so those conversations are naturally going to be behind closed doors.”

Roche also highlighted the launch of the Old Trafford Regeneration Mayoral Development Committee (MDC), which held its first meeting earlier this month.

The MDC, formed by local authorities Trafford Council and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority, will oversee the wider regeneration project of the Trafford area and has the power to force through a sale of land to United if necessary.

Lord Sebastian Coe, formerly head of the organising committee for the London 2012 Olympic Games, is the chair of the MDC, which also includes Andy Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester.

“They’re the ones that are going to help us with the planning, make sure we’ve got the infrastructure around the stadium to be able to get in and out efficiently and effectively, but also the ones that will remove any obstacles that we come up against as we go through this build, and to make sure that we can deliver the benefits,” Roche said. “As we’ve all said, we want to for the greater good.”

United unveiled their conceptual plans for a new, 100,000-seater stadium next to the existing Old Trafford site on 11 March last year, with Ratcliffe claiming that the vision could be realised within five years, by the start of the 2030-31 season.
